The test image is a microscopic view showing a large, round, dark brown/black sporangium on a sporangiophore with a collapsed apophysis structure - classic Rhizopus fungal morphology. This is a pathogen microscopy image, not a direct plant part view. Rhizopus_Soft_Rots is the primary candidate given these structures.

Now I'll view reference images across 4 different classes.

The Rhizopus_Soft_Rots reference shows fruit rot, but the test image (Bugwood 5369127) is microscopic. The Bugwood IDs are very close (5369119 vs 5369127), strongly suggesting the same source collection. Now checking Gray_Mold reference (Botrytis can also show spore structures microscopically).
Gray Mold reference shows macroscopic stem lesion - doesn't match the microscopic sporangium in the test image. Now checking Sclerotinia_Timber_Rot reference.
Sclerotinia shows macroscopic stem with sclerotia - doesn't match. Now checking the Rhizopus_Soft_Rots seed reference to confirm the microscopic sporangium link.

This is highly confirming. The Rhizopus_Soft_Rots/seed reference (Bugwood 5369124) shows numerous small dark sporangia on white mycelia. The test image (Bugwood 5369127) is from the same consecutive Bugwood image series (5369119, 5369124, 5369127), showing a close-up microscopic view of a single Rhizopus sporangium with its collapsed apophysis and sporangiophore.

Key evidence:
- Bugwood IDs are consecutive: 5369119 (pod rot), 5369124 (seed spores), 5369127 (test image) - all same source/collection
- Test image shows large, round, dark brown sporangium on a sporangiophore with collapsed apophysis - textbook Rhizopus morphology
- Symptom description: "whitish-gray mycelia with black sporangia" matches perfectly
- Gray Mold (Botrytis) produces grape-cluster conidia, not large spherical sporangia
- Sclerotinia produces sclerotia, not sporangia
